blocks.x: “You don’t have to set yourself on fire to keep other people warm.” ~Unknown

Tomorrow, a court will grant me a divorce after eleven years of marriage. I’ve spent the last several months rereading a decade of my own life like evidence in a case, trying to understand how I got here. What I found surprised me: not one dramatic betrayal, but hundreds of small moments where I chose to make myself smaller so the relationship could stay intact.

I met my husband when we were teenagers, through a mutual friend, and fell for him the way you fall for someone you’ve never actually met—through harmless texts and inside jokes, before either of us had to be a real, imperfect person in front of the other.

When I finally tried to meet him in real life, a year into our texting, his response to my suggestion was a cold “Why do you want to meet?” I remember the specific feeling—like a rug pulled out from under me—and I remember doing what I would keep doing for the next decade: deciding it was probably nothing, and staying.

Over the years there were more moments like that. A cutting remark dressed up as a joke, followed by an apology that reframed the remark rather than took it back. A pattern where any insecurity I voiced got returned to me as evidence that I was “too much,” while anything he needed became simply true, simply obvious, simply mine to accommodate.

None of it, on its own, seemed like a reason to leave. That’s the trouble with slow erosion—it never hands you a single moment dramatic enough to act on. It just quietly recalibrates what you think normal feels like.

I want to be honest about something, because I think it’s the part most people skip when they tell stories like this: I wasn’t only patient and wronged. I fought back, sometimes unfairly. I said things in anger I later regretted. I leaned on him more than was fair to either of us, treating him as my only anchor when I should have built more anchors of my own.

A good closure story isn’t the one where you were blameless. It’s the one where you can hold your own mistakes and someone else’s pattern of harm as two separate, simultaneous truths—without letting the first one erase the second.

The end came, as these things often do, without a single triggering event. He told me, out of nowhere, that he’d stopped loving me the way he used to, that he felt numb, that he needed space to “reevaluate.”

I spent the months after that doing what I imagine a lot of people do—trying to find the thread that would let me pull the relationship back together. I went to therapy. I read everything I could about attachment and communication. I joined a support group for people healing from relationships with emotionally unavailable or narcissistic partners, and for the first time, my ten years of specific, small, hard-to-explain moments started to form a legible pattern instead of a fog of self-doubt.
Even so, I did one more hard thing before I let myself close the door: I met him in person, one last time, so I could hear whatever he had to say without a screen or a delay between us.

Everyone in my support group warned me this might retraumatize me. I did it anyway, because I didn’t want to spend the rest of my life wondering if I’d walked away from something salvageable, or building a story about him that was kinder than the truth.

He talked for over two hours. He barely made eye contact. He told me our relationship had felt transactional to him, that he couldn’t remember much we’d built together besides travel—conveniently forgetting the books we read aloud to each other before sleeping, the audiobooks on long drives, the music medleys we made up together, the movies we cried through side by side.
When I asked him directly what he thought the best version of himself looked like, hoping for some flicker of reflection, he said, “Honestly, I think I am already the best version of me.”

That sentence did more to end my marriage than anything else in eleven years. Not because it was cruel—it wasn’t said cruelly at all—but because it told me, plainly, that there was no one on the other side of this relationship willing to keep growing alongside me. I had spent a decade trying to hold two people’s emotional development. I couldn’t keep doing that and remain a whole person myself.
Here is what I wish someone had told me earlier and what I hope reaches whoever needs it now:
A pattern is not the same as a phase.

If you find yourself, years into something, still waiting for someone to become emotionally available “once things settle down,” pay attention to how long “settling down” has already taken. Time doesn’t fix a capacity someone doesn’t have. Only they can build that, and only if they’re willing to look honestly at themselves—which is a decision no amount of your love can make for them.
You are allowed to trust your own memory.

For years, I doubted things I clearly remembered because they were met with confidence, or reframed, or simply denied. Writing my story down, in detail, with dates, was the thing that finally let me trust myself again. If you’re in something confusing, write it down as it happens. Future you will need the evidence, even if it’s only to convince yourself.
Protecting your peace is not the same as abandoning people who love you.

When my decision to divorce became final, friends and family, with love in their hearts, wanted to intervene, to talk to him, to try one more time. It hurt to say no to them. But I’ve learned that you can accept someone’s love without accepting their plan for your life. You’re allowed to say: I need you to trust that I’ve thought about this longer and harder than anyone else has. What I need from you now is support, not a rescue mission.
You can grieve something and still know leaving was right.

These aren’t in conflict, no matter what your last few doubt-filled nights tell you. I loved the version of us that existed in the good moments, and I also know that version was never going to be sustainable on its own. Holding both truths at once, instead of forcing myself to pick one, has been the most honest place I’ve found to grieve from.

Tomorrow, on paper, my marriage ends. In every way that matters, it ended months ago, in a park, in a two-and-a-half-hour monologue that finally gave me the clarity years of hoping never could. I’m not walking away from a marriage that could have been saved. I’m walking toward a version of my life where I stop being the only one doing the saving.
